summary: Manufacturing in Business Central covers production orders from creation to finish, posting of consumption, output, scrap and capacity, cost adjustment, and corrections. It also includes subcontracting and manufacturing analytics. It answers how-to and concept questions about running and costing production.
overview:
Manufacturing in Business Central plans, schedules, runs and analyzes production. The overview page explains the building blocks: production BOMs, routings, work and machine centers, and production orders. It is marked as part of the Premium experience.

The own pages follow the life of a production order. You create an order (source type item, family or sales order, with lines, copy and refresh), then record material consumption, output, run times and scrap. This can be done in the production journal or in batch journals, with flushing methods controlling when consumption posts. Capacity journals record work or machine center time outside production orders. When an order is finished, cost adjustment reconciles materials, capacity, subcontracting and overhead with WIP and inventory. A separate page covers reversing and correcting transactions.

Two subtopics go deeper. Subcontracting covers delegating operations to vendors, and Manufacturing analytics covers the Power BI Manufacturing app, production reports and capacity load. Start with the Manufacturing overview, then About production orders and Create production orders.
key_points: Production orders are created with a source type of item, family or sales order, with due dates, quantities, calculated start and end times, and lines that can be copied or refreshed.
Consumption can be flushed automatically or manually. Batch post consumption can calculate component usage and works with warehouse picks.
The Production Journal registers consumption, output, scrap and operation time for a released order in one place.
Batch post output and run times records quantities, setup and run time, scrap and stop codes, and uses routing explosion.
Scrap can be posted manually in the output journal with a quantity and scrap code to separate losses from good output.
Capacity journals post time for work or machine centers outside production orders, such as maintenance, to create capacity ledger entries.
A production order must be finished before its costs can be adjusted. Adjustment reconciles materials, capacity, subcontracting and overhead and calculates variances.
Transactions can be reversed: consumption, output and subcontracting receipts. Finished orders can be reopened or finished without output, with WIP write-off.
